demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: mentally rehearse worst case scenarios to feel prepared
Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively

issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: These trigger items are not clinically coherent with the indexed trauma of unexpected/traumatic death of a loved one. Snake-related and pregnancy/birth reminders imply trauma contexts unrelated to bereavement, and there is no supporting threat or memory content linking them to this loss.

issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: Avoiding military/police uniforms or weapons similarly implies a trauma context involving violence, combat, or armed threat, which is unsupported by the stated trauma type and by the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: For an index trauma of unexpected/traumatic death of a loved one, pregnancy/birth reminders are hard to justify unless the death specifically involved childbirth or infant loss; nothing else in the profile supports that context. This makes the trigger clinically implausible relative to the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons
issues.explanation: Avoiding military/police uniforms or weapons implies a trauma context involving combat, assault, or armed responders. That does not fit the rest of this bereavement-focused profile and is not supported by the other trigger, threat, or strategy items, so it appears incoherent with the trauma type and overall formulation.

vignette: Two years ago, Vikram Desai received a phone call that shattered his family's equilibrium: his younger brother, Arjun, had been killed instantly in a sudden, high-speed collision on the I-95. The violence of the crash and the abruptness of the loss fused into a lingering wound that refused to settle. At first, Vikram told himself he was simply mourning, but grief quickly curdled into a hyper-alert state. Whenever a client mentioned a relative's recent passing, or a design proposal required him to walk past a local cemetery, his chest would constrict before he could even process the conversation. His body would flare with readiness to flee, heart hammering against his ribs while his mind still tried to place the trigger. These sudden somatic surges, accompanied by brief but vivid flashbacks where the smell of burnt rubber and shattered glass would momentarily overtake the scent of fresh plaster, made him unable to finish the walkthrough. The threat response bypassed his reasoning entirely, leaving him standing in a client's foyer, dizzy and disoriented. To keep the panic at bay, Vikram began systematically erasing any date tied to October 14th from his calendar and avoiding any conversation that touched on loss. He rescheduled site visits to dodge the anniversary, convincing himself that a scheduling conflict was simply more professional. In his studio, surrounded by swatches and scale models, Vikram could no longer tolerate textures that felt too heavy or colors that leaned toward mourning blacks. He would strip the fabric samples from his mood boards the moment a client brought up a recent bereavement, his hands trembling as he replaced them with neutral tones. The avoidance felt necessary at the time, a way to shield his marriage and his firm's reputation from his unraveling composure. Yet, the mental space he tried to protect quickly filled with something worse. Lying awake in bed beside his wife, Priya, he would mentally rehearse worst-case scenarios-car crashes, sudden falls, hospital waiting rooms-trying to engineer a sense of control over an uncontrollable world. This relentless worst-case mental scripting only trained his nervous system to anticipate disaster, which in turn made his body react to minor stressors even faster. The cycle deepened across the following months. Every time a grief reminder slipped through his defenses, the resulting threat response pushed him further into preparation and avoidance, which only amplified his baseline alarm. He found himself snapping at Priya over misplaced keys, his irritability flaring into sharp, uncharacteristic outbursts that left him feeling guilty. Professionally, the strain became impossible to hide. When a long-time client, a widow grieving her husband, requested memorial pendants of dark marble for her new living room, Vikram's throat closed up and his vision blurred with that familiar, intrusive flash of Arjun's last moments. Fearing a collapse on the job site, he began declining any design project that required emotional labor, retreating to sterile, colorless spaces he could navigate without fear of breaking down. The constant rehearsal and avoidance had become a self-reinforcing trap, tightening his grip on his own life even as it frayed. By the second anniversary, the carefully constructed barriers had become a cage. Vikram's relentless mental preparation and his avoidance of any conversation touching on loss had drained his marriage of intimacy and threatened his firm's standing. He realized he could no longer outmaneuver the dread, nor could he explain why his hands shook every time a news report mentioned a highway accident. Seeking help felt like admitting the walls he had built were failing. He walked into the clinic hoping to dismantle the loop before it cost him his career or his marriage, desperate to find a way to remember his brother without feeling like he was dying all over again.
